dimension: Rating and ranking systems that produce an ordering from pairwise outcomes (Elo, Glicko, TrueSkill, Bradley-Terry/Plackett-Luce, tournament design, and the sample-efficiency and lock-in literature)
summary:
This field has solved the founder's cold-start problem explicitly and has measured his tournament idea to be the worst of the available formats. Three findings dominate.

First, cold start is a solved problem, and the solution is an uncertainty state carried alongside the rating. Glicko gives an unrated player rating 1500 and rating deviation (RD) 350, and RD shrinks only as games are played (Glickman, "The Glicko system", glicko.net/glicko/glicko.pdf; Applied Statistics 48:377-394, 1999). Running Glickman's own equations (my script, /private/tmp/.../scratchpad/glicko_rd_games.py): from RD 350 against equally-rated established opponents, 12 games reach RD 100, 48 games reach RD 50, 135 games reach RD 30. That is the honest cost of ranking a roster, per participant. The founder's 2 mechanisms produce 1 observation per participant per round; a knockout gives half the roster exactly 1 game ever.

Second, his knockout is measured as the least effective format. Exact computation for 8 players found single knockout the least effective at identifying the best player (David 1959; Glenn 1960; Searls 1963, as reviewed by Devriesere, Csató and Goossens, arXiv:2404.05034). At equal match count, the Swiss system beats knockout and group formats, especially at reproducing the full ranking (Sziklai, Biró and Csató, Computers & Operations Research 144:105821, 2022; arXiv:2103.06023). Worse, the Bradley-Terry maximum-likelihood estimate does not exist on a bracket: Ford's (1957) strong-connectivity condition cannot hold on an acyclic win graph. Measured over 500 simulated 16-player tournaments (my script bt_connect_rate.py): knockout 0/500 estimable, 10-round Swiss 239/500.

Third, lock-in has a precise answer, and it is not the one he fears. Glicko-2's volatility rises on "exceptionally strong results after a period of stability", widening subsequent updates; TrueSkill adds a dynamics factor each match that the reference implementation calls "the factor that restrains a fixation of rating". But no relative rating system can detect a uniform population improvement, because strengths are identified only up to an additive constant. That is exactly the measured FIDE deflation episode.

mechanisms.name: Elo rating system
mechanisms.what_it_does: Single scalar per participant, updated after each result by K times (actual minus expected score), with expected score a logistic function of the rating difference. Király and Qian showed the update is an online stochastic-gradient step on the Bradley-Terry log-likelihood; Tang, Wang and Jin recast it as online gradient descent on binary cross-entropy with regret bound Regret_T <= (3/2)GD*sqrt(T) (Theorem 1) and per-round bound C*sqrt(N/T) at learning rate eta_t = sqrt(N/t).
mechanisms.citation: Elo, A.E., The Rating of Chessplayers, Past and Present, 1978. Király, F.J. and Qian, Z., 'Modelling Competitive Sports: Bradley-Terry-Élő Models for Supervised and On-Line Learning of Paired Competition Outcomes', arXiv:1701.08055, 2017. Tang, S., Wang, Y. and Jin, C., 'Is Elo Rating Reliable? A Study Under Model Misspecification', arXiv:2502.10985, 16 Feb 2025.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Badly, and this is the documented reason Glicko exists. Elo carries no uncertainty state, so it cannot distinguish a rating of 1700 that is unknown from one that is precisely measured. Glickman's motivating example: two players both rated 1700, one returning after years away, one playing weekly; plain USCF Elo moves both by exactly 16 points. The only lever is the K-factor, which is a global constant, not a per-participant confidence.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Not at all in the resource sense. Elo assumes every match costs the same and every outcome carries the same information. It has no notion of a participant's compute budget, price, or latency, and no notion of an asymmetric match cost.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Do not use plain Elo as the estimator. Two independent measurements say the choice among Elo-family systems barely matters once data is adequate — on a real arena dataset cumulative loss was Elo 0.6607, Glicko 0.6602, TrueSkill 0.6611, Elo2k 0.6611, Pairwise 0.6619 (Tang et al. 2025, Table 2), and on 1087 contests of ~2999 participants each, pairwise-inversion accuracy was 78.3% / 78.5% / 61.7% / 78.5% / 78.6% for Codeforces / TopCoder / TrueSkill / Elo-MMχ / Elo-MMR (Ebtekar and Liu 2021, Table 2). What DOES matter is the uncertainty state and the pairing rule. Elo's value to CDSFL is as the diagnostic baseline, not the engine.

mechanisms.name: Glicko (rating deviation)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Adds a rating deviation RD, a posterior standard deviation on the rating. Unrated: rating 1500, RD 350. Between periods of inactivity RD = min(sqrt(RD_old^2 + c^2*t), 350). After a period of m games, RD' = (1/RD^2 + 1/d^2)^(-1/2) with d^-2 = q^2 * sum_j g(RD_j)^2 E_j(1-E_j), q = ln(10)/400. Rating changes are NOT symmetric: how much the loser drops depends on both players' RDs.
mechanisms.citation: Glickman, M.E., 'Parameter estimation in large dynamic paired comparison experiments', Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series C (Applied Statistics) 48(3):377-394, 1999, DOI 10.1111/1467-9876.00159. Working description with all equations: https://www.glicko.net/glicko/glicko.pdf
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: This IS the cold-start mechanism, and it is explicit. A new participant starts at 1500 with RD 350, which is a 95% credible interval of plus or minus 686 rating points — i.e. the system states in its own units that it knows nothing. Each game shrinks RD; I ran Glickman's equations directly (scratchpad/glicko_rd_games.py, against equally-rated opponents of RD 30): 1 game -> RD 247, 5 -> 143, 12 -> below 100, 48 -> below 50, 135 -> below 30. Glickman's own guidance is 5 to 10 games per player per rating period. The founder gets the ranking he wants without any staged difficulty ladder: he just has to pay for roughly 12 to 48 observations per model, not 1.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Partially, and in a way that directly answers his desktop-versus-supercomputer objection. A mismatched pairing is not forbidden, it is simply low-information, and the system quantifies that: Glicko downweights a result against a high-RD opponent via g(RD), and the Fisher information of a single Bradley-Terry comparison is p(1-p), maximised at p = 0.5. I verified this symbolically (SymPy, same script): argmax at p = 1/2, value 1/4; a pairing where the favourite wins 90% of the time yields 0.09, so 2.78 times less information per match, and at 99% it is 0.0099, i.e. 25.3 times less. So pitting a desktop against a supercomputer is not unfair, it is wasteful — you pay a full match for 4% of an even match's information.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers directly and should be the default. The RD is exactly the 'measured capability, never a name' guarantee the founder wants, expressed as an interval rather than a point. What breaks if adopted: (1) CDSFL must accept that a model with few observations carries a wide interval and must not be routed as if its rating were known — the RD has to reach the router, not just the leaderboard; (2) Glicko assumes a central authority computing one update per rating period over all results, which conflicts with the peer-to-peer requirement; (3) Glicko is single-scalar, so cost and capability cannot both live in it.

mechanisms.name: Glicko-2 (rating volatility)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Adds a third per-participant parameter, volatility sigma, defaulting to 0.06 for an unrated player (rating 1500, RD 350). Sigma is high when a participant has erratic performances — Glickman names the case explicitly: 'exceptionally strong results after a period of stability' — and low when performance is consistent. A system constant tau constrains how fast sigma can move; Glickman recommends 0.3 to 1.2, and as low as 0.2 where very improbable result sets are expected. On inactivity, phi' = sqrt(phi^2 + sigma^2).
mechanisms.citation: Glickman, M.E., 'Dynamic paired comparison models with stochastic variances', Journal of Applied Statistics 28:673-689, 2001. Worked example and all 8 steps: Glickman, 'Example of the Glicko-2 system', Boston University, 22 March 2022, http://www.glicko.net/glicko/glicko2.pdf
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Same as Glicko (1500 / 350) plus an initial volatility of 0.06, which Glickman notes 'depends on the particular application'. Glicko-2 wants a larger rating period than Glicko: at least 10 to 15 games per player, versus 5 to 10.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Same information-geometry treatment as Glicko. Note that in the update, 'the opponents' volatilities are not relevant' — only their ratings and RDs enter. So a volatile opponent does not contaminate your estimate, which matters when some participants in a heterogeneous roster are being reconfigured mid-run.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the direct, published answer to the founder's lock-in worry, and it should be stated to him in these terms. If a model's capability jumps 10-fold, its results become 'exceptionally strong after a period of stability', volatility rises, RD widens, and subsequent updates get larger — the system self-unlocks. The cost is a tuning decision: tau small enough that one freak run does not catapult a model, large enough that a real step change is tracked within a few rating periods. What breaks: tau is a global constant and must be fitted by predictive accuracy, which means CDSFL needs a held-out set of historical results before it can set it, and cannot set it on day 1.

mechanisms.name: TrueSkill and TrueSkill 2
mechanisms.what_it_does: Bayesian skill rating by factor-graph message passing (expectation propagation): each participant holds a Gaussian (mu, sigma). Common defaults are mu 25, sigma 25/3, beta 25/6 (the skill gap giving roughly a 76% win chance), tau 25/300 as the per-match dynamics term, and a 10% draw rate. TrueSkill 2 adds experience, squad membership, score margin, quit tendency, and skill in other modes.
mechanisms.citation: Herbrich, R., Minka, T. and Graepel, T., 'TrueSkill(TM): A Bayesian Skill Rating System', NIPS 19, 2007 (MSR-TR-2006-80). Minka, T., Cleven, R. and Zaykov, Y., 'TrueSkill 2: An improved Bayesian skill rating system', Microsoft Research Technical Report MSR-TR-2018-8, March 2018, https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2018/03/trueskill2.pdf. Parameter semantics and the 'restrains a fixation of rating' description of tau: https://trueskill.org/
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Two mechanisms. (1) A wide prior sigma that narrows with play; Microsoft's own product page gives a minimum of 12 games per gamer for 2-player free-for-all, 10 for 4 teams of 2, and 91 for 2 teams of 8 — a product claim, not a derivation, but it is the right order and it matches my Glicko computation of 12 games to RD 100. (2) TrueSkill 2 solves cold start by TRANSFER: it borrows a player's rating from other game modes when they start a new one. That is the published version of what CDSFL would want — bootstrap a model's rating on a new task family from its measured rating on others. Measured payoff on one title: 68% historical-match prediction accuracy versus 52% for TrueSkill.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: TrueSkill is the only mainstream system built for multi-team, multi-player, unequal-team-size matches, which is the closest published analogue to heterogeneous participants contributing unequally to a joint outcome. But it degrades badly when there are many distinct ranks in one round: Ebtekar and Liu measured 61.7% pairwise-inversion accuracy against 78.3% for alternatives on contests with thousands of participants, and report 'TrueSkill and Elo-MMR score about equally when the number of ranks is less than about 60'.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Use the TrueSkill 2 transfer idea, not the TrueSkill engine, if the roster can exceed about 60 simultaneously-ranked participants. TrueSkill's message passing is inherently sequential and was not parallelisable in Ebtekar and Liu's own hands. What breaks if adopted wholesale: at 70 or 700 models ranked in one round, the measured accuracy collapse above about 60 distinct ranks hits CDSFL squarely, and the founder's stated requirement is 700.

mechanisms.name: Bradley-Terry / Bradley-Terry-Luce and its MLE (Ford's condition, Hunter's MM)
mechanisms.what_it_does: P(i beats j) = w_i/(w_i + w_j), equivalently a logistic function of a strength difference. Fitted by maximum likelihood, in practice by Hunter's minorization-maximization iteration, which converges to the global maximum for the basic model. Ford (1957) gives the necessary AND sufficient condition for a finite, unique MLE: for every split of the items into two non-empty groups, someone in one group has beaten someone in the other — i.e. the directed win graph is strongly connected.
mechanisms.citation: Bradley, R.A. and Terry, M.E., 'Rank analysis of incomplete block designs: I. The method of paired comparisons', Biometrika 39:324-345, 1952 (Zermelo 1929 is the prior independent derivation; see 'The many routes to the ubiquitous Bradley-Terry model', arXiv:2312.13619). Ford, L.R., 'Solution of a ranking problem from binary comparisons', American Mathematical Monthly 64:28-33, 1957. Hunter, D.R., 'MM algorithms for generalized Bradley-Terry models', Annals of Statistics 32(1):384-406, 2004. Failure case and penalised fix: Yan, T., 'Ranking in the generalized Bradley-Terry models when the strong connection condition fails', arXiv:1411.1168.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: It does not. The unregularised BT MLE has no prior, so a participant with 0 games has no estimate and a participant who has only won has an estimate of plus infinity. Cold start must be handled by a prior (which is what Glicko, TrueSkill and the arena's reweighted fit all do) or by a penalty (Yan's epsilon singular perturbation).
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: The model is scale-free in strength but says nothing about cost. It is also identified only up to a multiplicative constant on w (hence Ford's normalisation 1'w = 1), which is the mathematical root of the inflation/deflation problem below.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: THIS IS THE HARD BLOCKER ON THE KNOCKOUT IDEA, and it is a theorem, not a preference. A single-elimination bracket on n players produces exactly n-1 matches and an ACYCLIC win graph, so Ford's condition can never hold for n >= 2 and the BT MLE does not exist. I measured it (scratchpad/bt_connect_rate.py, 500 simulated 16-player tournaments per configuration, logistic true-skill model): knockout gave an estimable MLE in 0 of 500 runs at every noise level tested; Hunter's MM iteration diverged to a max/min strength ratio of 1.6e+301. A 7-round Swiss on the same 16 players gave 65 of 500 at upset-scale 4.0, 132 of 500 at scale 8.0, 5 of 500 at scale 2.0; a 10-round Swiss gave 239 of 500. So neither format reliably yields a defined MLE, and the correct conclusion is not 'use Swiss instead' but 'never use an unregularised BT MLE' — use a Bayesian or penalised estimator, which is what every production system does.

mechanisms.name: Plackett-Luce model
mechanisms.what_it_does: Extends Bradley-Terry from pairs to full or partial RANKINGS: the probability of an ordering is the product of successive 'choose the next item in proportion to its strength' probabilities, from Luce's choice axiom (the odds between two items do not depend on which others are present). Handles complete rankings, partial rankings, and top-k-only observations.
mechanisms.citation: Luce, R.D., Individual Choice Behavior: A Theoretical Analysis, Wiley, 1959. Plackett, R.L., 'The analysis of permutations', Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series C (Applied Statistics) 24(2):193-202, 1975. Bayesian inference: Guiver, J. and Snelson, E., 'Bayesian inference for Plackett-Luce ranking models', ICML 2009, DOI 10.1145/1553374.1553423.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Same limitation as Bradley-Terry without a prior; Guiver and Snelson's Power-EP treatment supplies one. Its cold-start ADVANTAGE is informational: one round in which m participants are ranked against each other yields m(m-1)/2 pairwise constraints rather than m/2, so a single free-for-all round on the whole roster is worth far more than a single bracket round.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Luce's axiom is also the model's weakness here: independence from irrelevant alternatives means it cannot represent 'model A beats B only when C is also in the pool'. It also makes it manipulable by cloning — adding near-duplicate participants shifts the estimates.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the right likelihood for CDSFL's actual observation unit. CDSFL does not generate 1-versus-1 duels; it generates a round in which several seats attempt the same claim and can be ORDERED by who solved it, how fast, with what proof, and at what cost. That is a partial ranking, which is exactly Plackett-Luce's data type. What breaks: the irrelevant-alternatives assumption is wrong for a falsification harness where one seat's output is visible to another, so seat isolation becomes a modelling requirement, not just a hygiene one.

mechanisms.name: Elo-MMR (massive multiplayer ratings)
mechanisms.what_it_does: A Bayesian system generalising Glicko to an unbounded number of simultaneously-ranked participants, deriving closed-form updates by taking the limit as participation goes to infinity. Proves three properties: aligned incentives (Theorem 5.5 — a player maximising their rating never wants to place lower), robustness (Theorem 5.7 — bounded rating change per contest, of order sigma_t^2/beta_t to beta_0^2/beta_t), and runtime O(sum_i (|P| + |H_i|) log log(1/eps)), reduced to O((|P|/eps^2) log log(1/eps)) with adaptive opponent subsampling and history compression.
mechanisms.citation: Ebtekar, A. and Liu, P., 'Elo-MMR: A Rating System for Massive Multiplayer Competitions', The Web Conference (WWW) 2021, DOI 10.1145/3442381.3450091; arXiv:2101.00400. Implementation: https://github.com/EbTech/Elo-MMR
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Inherits Glicko's prior-plus-uncertainty treatment and adds a 'pseudodiffusion' step that preserves momentum between contests while provably not breaking incentive alignment. Validated on 1087 contests averaging 2999 participants each, plus a 1000-thread social dataset averaging 20 participants, plus a 10000-player synthetic set.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Built for exactly the roster-size range the founder specified: it handles 1, 5, 70 or 700 participants per round with runtime scaling linearly in participants, and was shown to process the entire history of a 300000-rated-user platform on a laptop in under half an hour. It beat the two incumbent platform systems by nearly an order of magnitude in compute on the larger dataset (212.9 s and 72.5 s versus 31.4 s and 35.4 s).
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: The closest off-the-shelf fit to CDSFL's stated constraints, and I would recommend it over TrueSkill for a large roster. Its incentive-alignment theorem matters more for CDSFL than for chess: a seat that can gain rating by underperforming is a seat that can game a falsification harness, and Elo-MMR is the only system in this literature with a PROOF (the authors state TrueSkill is 'believed to satisfy the first two properties, albeit without proof, but fails robustness'). What breaks: the adaptive-subsampling optimisation chooses different opponents per participant, and the authors warn that 'if the setting requires aligned incentives to hold exactly, then one must avoid choosing different opponents for each player' — so CDSFL must choose between exact incentive alignment and the 1/eps^2 speedup.

mechanisms.name: Swiss system, score groups, and accelerated (Baku) pairings
mechanisms.what_it_does: A fixed number of rounds, far fewer than the n-1 of a round robin, with each round pairing participants of equal or near-equal cumulative score, no elimination, and no rematches. Within a score group the Dutch system splits top and bottom halves and pairs 1-versus-5, 2-versus-6 and so on. Accelerated pairings (FIDE's Baku system) give the top half of the field virtual extra points FOR PAIRING ONLY across the first half of the rounds — a full point for the first half of the accelerated rounds, a half point for the rest — explicitly excluded from the standings.
mechanisms.citation: FIDE Handbook Chapter C.04: C.04.1 Basic rules for Swiss Systems, C.04.2 General handling rules, C.04.3 FIDE (Dutch) System, current versions effective 1 February 2026 (approved by FIDE Council 28 October 2025), https://handbook.fide.com/chapter/C0403202602 [VERIFY:current — the handbook is revised periodically]. First used at Zürich, 1895.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Round 1 has no scores, so pairing falls back to the initial order (normally the prior rating) split into halves, with colours decided by lot. With NO prior at all this degenerates to a random pairing — which means the founder's 'names drawn from a bag' is precisely the FIDE round-1 rule under an uninformative prior, and is correct for round 1 only. Rounds 2 onwards use the accumulated score, which is where the knockout throws information away and Swiss does not.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: The score group IS the self-organising league the founder is reaching for, and it is strictly better than a persistent league because it is recomputed every round and therefore cannot lock in. Accelerated pairings exist for exactly his worry about wasting early rounds on mismatches: they bias early pairings toward the presumed-strong half without contaminating the standings.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Adopt the Swiss skeleton rather than a bracket. At equal match count it is the measured best format for recovering a full ranking (see tournament-efficacy entry). Its stated reasons transfer verbatim: it does not eliminate a participant after a single loss (satisfying the founder's 'no model permanently set aside' constraint by construction) and it uses the history of comparisons. Also note Sziklai et al.'s warning that 'comparing the same pair of players multiple times is wasteful', which the no-rematch rule enforces. What breaks: Swiss needs a central pairing authority each round, which conflicts with the no-central-server requirement, and the greedy pairing can fail to pair everyone when the no-rematch constraint binds (observed in my own simulation: 55 matches delivered where 56 were expected).

mechanisms.name: Tournament-format efficacy: knockout versus round robin versus Swiss
mechanisms.what_it_does: A 65-year literature measuring the probability that a format identifies the true best participant ('effectivity' or 'predictive power') and the true full ranking ('efficacy'), by exact combinatorics for small n and Monte Carlo otherwise.
mechanisms.citation: David, H.A. (1959); Glenn, W.A. (1960); Searls, D.T. (1963) — exact winning probabilities for 8-player single knockout and single round robin. Ryvkin, D. and Ortmann, A., 'The Predictive Power of Three Prominent Tournament Formats', Management Science 54(3):492-504, 2008, DOI 10.1287/mnsc.1070.0856. Sziklai, B.R., Biró, P. and Csató, L., 'The efficacy of tournament designs', Computers & Operations Research 144:105821, 2022; arXiv:2103.06023. Lahvička, J. (2015a) on playoffs. Vu, T. and Shoham, Y. (2011) and Arlegi, R. and Dimitrov, D. (2020) on the impossibility result. Survey with all of the above: Devriesere, K., Csató, L. and Goossens, D., 'Tournament design: A review from an operational research perspective', arXiv:2404.05034.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Treats the prior as an input, and measures how much it is worth. Sziklai et al.: 'the benefit of seeding strongly depends on the accuracy of the prior information' — with no accurate prior, seeding buys little, which supports the founder's instinct to assume no capability. But their headline result is that what you do with the results AFTER round 1 matters far more than the round-1 draw.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Measures it directly. Sziklai et al. found the Swiss advantage is LARGER when the field is less balanced (tennis) and smallest when it is balanced (chess). A heterogeneous roster of 1 to 700 participants of wildly varying capability is the less-balanced case, so the Swiss advantage over knockout is larger for CDSFL than for chess, not smaller.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Four concrete numbers the founder should see. (1) Single knockout was found the LEAST effective of the formats studied for 8 players; double and serial knockout are better, best-of-3 matches better still (David 1959, Glenn 1960, Searls 1963). (2) At 32 players, a 5-round Swiss has 80 matches — exactly the same as a single knockout — and the Swiss recovers the full ranking better (Sziklai et al. 2022). (3) Adding a knockout playoff AFTER a double round robin cut the probability that the strongest team wins from 48% to 39% (Lahvička 2015a) — elimination actively destroys accuracy. (4) An impossibility theorem: a BALANCED knockout with 8 or more players cannot simultaneously guarantee that stronger participants are favoured over weaker ones AND that equally strong participants are treated equally (Vu and Shoham 2011; Arlegi and Dimitrov 2020). The founder's random bracket therefore cannot be made fair and accurate at once, as a matter of proof. One honest caveat: for picking a SOLE winner (not a full ranking), knockout and draw-and-process remain competitive with Swiss, especially when the stronger participant almost always wins. If CDSFL only ever needs 'who is top', the bracket is less bad than it looks. It needs a full ranking for tiered resource allocation, so it does not.

mechanisms.name: Adaptive paired-comparison design (optimal pairing by expected information gain)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Chooses the whole round's pairings to maximise the expected Kullback-Leibler divergence from prior to posterior, which decomposes into a sum of per-game contributions and is therefore solvable as a weighted graph matching. The decisive result: the per-game contribution C_ij is largest when the two participants' expected strength difference is near ZERO and the standard deviation of that difference is LARGE.
mechanisms.citation: Glickman, M.E. and Jensen, S.T., 'Adaptive paired comparison design', Journal of Statistical Planning and Inference 127(1-2):279-293, 2005, DOI 10.1016/j.jspi.2003.09.022. Full text: https://faculty.wharton.upenn.edu/wp-content/uploads/2012/04/Shanejensen.tourney05.pdf
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Head on, and with a measured answer for the founder's exact case. Under a NON-INFORMATIVE prior (50 players, prior variances 4, means a random permutation — i.e. 'assume no capability'), log posterior determinant over 500 simulations was: random pairing 13.13, Swiss 8.69, information-optimal 8.28 at 4 rounds; and -42.63 / -54.96 / -57.73 at 16 rounds. Sum of squared rank deviation from truth at 4 rounds: random 5557, Swiss 3714, optimal 5201. So even with NO prior, random pairing is the worst of the three on both criteria, and Swiss beats the information-optimal rule on rank recovery in the early rounds.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: It is the formal reason not to pitch a desktop against a supercomputer: the criterion says a lopsided pairing contributes little information. I verified the underlying quantity symbolically — the Fisher information of a Bradley-Terry comparison, p(1-p), peaks at 1/4 for p = 0.5 and falls to 0.0099 at p = 0.99, a factor of 25.3 (scratchpad/glicko_rd_games.py).
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the citation that settles the founder's 'is random pairing the same as uninformative?' question. The precise answer: at round 1 with a genuinely exchangeable prior, random IS optimal — all pairings have identical expected utility by symmetry, so there is nothing to choose. From round 2 onward random is strictly suboptimal, and the measured gap widens with rounds. The rule is to pair participants whose estimated capability is CLOSE and whose uncertainty is LARGE. What breaks if adopted: Glickman and Jensen note their rule 'is not optimized to produce rankings that are consistent with the truth in small numbers of rounds', because pairing near-equals deliberately produces coin-flip outcomes that shuffle the means. If CDSFL needs a usable ranking after 4 rounds rather than a precise one after 16, Swiss score groups are the better choice.

mechanisms.name: Dueling bandits and active match scheduling for top-k identification
mechanisms.what_it_does: Treats 'which pair to compare next' as a bandit problem over pairs with only binary comparison feedback, maintaining a candidate set by upper-confidence bound and comparing the pair with the highest outcome uncertainty. MaxIn-Elo does this on top of the gradient Elo update, achieving O~(sqrt(T)) regret with O(n^2) memory and constant per-step cost, versus O(t) time for MLE-based schemes.
mechanisms.citation: Yue, Y., Broder, J., Kleinberg, R. and Joachims, T., 'The K-armed dueling bandits problem', Journal of Computer and System Sciences 78(5):1538-1556, 2012. Yan, X., Du, Y., Ru, B., Wang, J., Zhang, H. and Chen, X., 'Learning to Identify Top Elo Ratings: A Dueling Bandits Approach', AAAI-22, pp. 8797-8805. Also Ren, W., Liu, J. and Shroff, N., 'The sample complexity of best-k items selection from pairwise comparisons', ICML 2020; Mohajer, S., Suh, C. and Elmahdy, A., 'Active learning for top-k rank aggregation from noisy comparisons', ICML 2017.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Explicitly: the UCB bonus is large for unobserved participants, so an unmeasured model is scheduled for comparison because it is uncertain, not because anyone believes it is good. That is the founder's constraint ('capability is measured, never a name') implemented as an algorithm. The PAC sample-complexity order for the pairwise setting is O((n/eps^2) log(n/(eps*delta))), with a matching lower bound of order (n/eps^2) ln(1/delta).
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Top-k formulations match CDSFL's actual need exactly: the system does not need a correct ordering of the bottom 600 models, only a correct TOP TIER. Sample complexity for top-k is much lower than for a full ranking, which is the single biggest cost saving available to CDSFL and is not in either of the founder's mechanisms.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Yan et al. name the founder's two mechanisms and reject both for the same reason: 'both the Round-robin and the Elimination tournament organise competitions following a pre-designed schedule, and the Elimination tournament scheduling may need some prior knowledge on the players' skill. Also each pair of players only compete once in both schemes so the results can be highly noisy.' Their alternative is to allocate comparisons where uncertainty is highest among top candidates. What breaks if adopted: adaptive scheduling is precisely what Elo's consistency guarantee does NOT survive (see the misspecification entry), so CDSFL cannot adopt adaptive scheduling and keep a naive Elo estimator — it must adopt both the adaptive schedule and an estimator that corrects for it.

mechanisms.name: Sample complexity of ranking from pairwise comparisons (Rank Centrality)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Scores items by the stationary distribution of a random walk on the comparison graph whose edge weights are win fractions. Upper bound: with comparisons between omega(n log n) randomly chosen pairs under a BTL model, it learns the true scores to arbitrary accuracy with high probability. Lower bound: Omega(n log n) random comparisons are NECESSARY for ANY algorithm, because below that the comparison graph is disconnected with positive probability. For a general comparison graph the bound becomes O(xi^-2 * n * polylog(n)) where xi is the spectral gap of the graph Laplacian.
mechanisms.citation: Negahban, S., Oh, S. and Shah, D., 'Rank Centrality: Ranking from Pairwise Comparisons', Operations Research 65(1):266-287, 2017; arXiv:1209.1688 (NIPS 2012 precursor: 'Iterative ranking from pair-wise comparisons').
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Gives the budget, which is what the founder actually asked for. For n participants you need order n log n comparisons, not n. For n = 700 that is roughly 700 * log(700) ~ 4600 comparisons as an order-of-magnitude floor; a knockout on 700 gives 699. His bracket is short of the information-theoretic lower bound by a factor of about 6.6, and that bound is for ANY algorithm.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: The spectral-gap form is the key result for a heterogeneous roster: if the comparison graph is poorly connected — which is exactly what happens when a tiered ladder stops comparing across tiers — the required number of comparisons blows up as xi^-2. A league structure that forbids cross-tier matches directly degrades the spectral gap and therefore the sample complexity.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers as the budgeting rule and as the argument against hard tier boundaries. CDSFL should hold out a fraction of comparisons for cross-tier pairings purely to keep the comparison graph well connected, even though those pairings are individually low-information by the Fisher criterion. That is a genuine tension the literature exposes: Glickman-Jensen says pair near-equals, Negahban-Oh-Shah says keep the graph connected, and the resolution is a mixture, not a pure strategy.

mechanisms.name: Reweighted Bradley-Terry MLE with active sampling (the LLM arena stack)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Fits Bradley-Terry by maximum likelihood with each observation inverse-weighted by its sampling probability, so the estimand is a uniform distribution over model pairs despite non-uniform sampling; produces simultaneous confidence sets via sandwich robust standard errors and a chi-squared interval. Samples pairs in proportion to the expected reduction in each pair's confidence-interval width.
mechanisms.citation: Chiang, W.-L., Zheng, L., Sheng, Y., Angelopoulos, A.N., Li, T., Li, D., Zhang, H., Zhu, B., Jordan, M., Gonzalez, J.E. and Stoica, I., 'Chatbot Arena: An Open Platform for Evaluating LLMs by Human Preference', arXiv:2403.04132 (ICML 2024), Section 5, Equation 9. Sampling-asymmetry critique: Singh, S., Nan, Y., Wang, A. et al., 'The Leaderboard Illusion', arXiv:2504.20879, NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks track.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: By reporting an interval rather than a rank, and by actively sampling the pairs whose intervals are widest — a new entrant is sampled because it is uncertain. The measured sample-efficiency gain of active over random sampling is a useful reality check on how much clever pairing is worth: for win-matrix precision 0.2, random needed about 6800 samples versus about 4400 adaptive (random needs roughly 54% more); but for Bradley-Terry SCORE precision 0.3 it was about 17200 versus about 16400, only about 5% more. The scale: roughly 240000 votes (243329 conversations) across more than 50 models from over 90000 users, as of January 2024.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: The inverse-probability reweighting is the mechanism that makes a heterogeneous, unevenly-sampled roster comparable, and the Leaderboard Illusion paper is the measured demonstration of what happens without it: peak daily sampling rates ranged from 34% down to 3.3% across providers, two providers received an estimated 19.2% and 20.4% of all data while open-source models collectively received 8.8%, and 205 of 243 public models had been silently deprecated.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: The reweighting is non-negotiable for CDSFL and is the single most actionable import. The moment CDSFL routes more work to models it believes are strong, its own rating data becomes non-uniformly sampled, and an unweighted fit will confirm its prior. The honest counterweight: the arena's own measurement says active sampling buys only about 5% on score precision, so CDSFL should not spend engineering effort on a clever scheduler before it has spent it on the reweighting and the uncertainty intervals. What breaks: the Leaderboard Illusion authors report that the arena's own published sampling rule 'appears not to be respected or implemented in practice' — a warning that the correction is easy to specify and easy to quietly not apply, which is exactly the failure mode CDSFL's own record is full of.

mechanisms.name: Order dependence and transitivity failure of Elo on static entities
mechanisms.what_it_does: Measures Elo's reliability (invariance to the order of comparisons) and transitivity when the entities being rated have FIXED rather than evolving capability, by re-running the same fixed set of match outcomes under many random permutations of their order.
mechanisms.citation: Boubdir, M., Kim, E., Ermis, B., Hooker, S. and Fadaee, M., 'Elo Uncovered: Robustness and Best Practices in Language Model Evaluation', arXiv:2311.17295, 29 November 2023 (Cohere for AI).
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Not its subject, but it bears on it: at Nperms = 1 (a single sequence, which is what one tournament is) Elo ratings are unstable, 'especially for winning probabilities nearing 0.5' and the instability is 'markedly exacerbated at higher K-factors'. Instability plateaus once Nperms exceeds 100.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Shows the problem is worst for NEAR-EQUAL participants: where win rates differ a lot the ratings are consistent across K and Nperms; where models perform similarly the rankings are sensitive to both hyperparameters.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: The recommendation is explicit and directly contradicts a single-bracket design: 'To obtain stable and reliable Elo ratings, it's recommended to run numerous permutations, ideally with Nperm >= 100.' A knockout tournament is Nperms = 1 by construction — the bracket IS one ordering, and the authors measured that one ordering is not enough. They also found transitivity 'is not universally conserved', with discrepancies in model rankings at Nperms = 100 and K = 1 and more consistent rankings at K = 16, i.e. too small a K is 'too conservative to capture the transitive relations quickly'. What breaks for CDSFL: if the models being ranked have static capability, CDSFL should either re-run the aggregation over many permutations of its result log, or use a batch (order-free) estimator like the Bradley-Terry MLE with a prior, rather than an online sequential update. The batch route is also the one that lets CDSFL re-derive ratings from an immutable result log, which fits its evidence discipline.

mechanisms.name: Urnings (the only rating algorithm that corrects for adaptive selection)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Represents each rating as coloured balls in an urn, with updates designed so the invariant distribution is binomial with the urn size as the number of trials and the inverse-logit of the latent ability as the success probability, conditional on the total. Because the limiting distribution is KNOWN, exact uncertainty quantification is available rather than an approximation. Includes an explicit correction for adaptive item/opponent selection, and an Item Paired Update Procedure to keep the latent scale from drifting.
mechanisms.citation: Bolsinova, M., Maris, G., Hofman, A.D., van der Maas, H.L.J. and Brinkhuis, M.J.S., 'Urnings: A new method for tracking dynamically changing parameters in paired comparison systems', Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series C (Applied Statistics) 71(1):91-118, 2022. Multidimensional extension: Bolsinova et al., 'Tracking a multitude of abilities as they develop', British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology, 2022, DOI 10.1111/bmsp.12276. Cold-start extension: 'Warming up the Cold Start: Adaptive Step Size Method for the Urnings Algorithm', AIED 2023, DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-36336-8_64.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: There is a dedicated paper on it, because the original algorithm did not address cold start: an adaptive step-size method for the case where selection is poorly tuned to ability at the start. The urn size sets the resolution-versus-adaptivity trade-off explicitly, which is a cleaner control surface than Glicko's c and tau.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: The multidimensional version tracks several interrelated abilities per participant, at both individual and population level, with between-item and within-item multidimensionality. That is the closest published machinery to CDSFL's need to rate a model on several capability axes rather than one scalar.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the most important single finding in this dimension for CDSFL's actual design, because it names a defect that every other system in this list shares. The authors state that adaptive selection 'leads to inflation of the variance, meaning that the ratings are diverging from each other over time without converging to a limiting distribution', and a follow-up states that Urnings is, to their knowledge, 'the only [algorithm] that incorporates a correction for adaptive item selection' — explicitly excluding Glicko (2001), TrueSkill (2006) and TrueSkill 2 (2018). CDSFL's whole design intent is adaptive selection: route hard claims to strong seats, easy claims to cheap seats. If it does that and rates with Glicko or TrueSkill, the ratings will spread without converging, and the top tier will look increasingly separated from the rest for reasons that are an artefact of the routing, not a measurement of capability. That is a self-confirming leaderboard, which is the exact failure the founder is trying to avoid.

mechanisms.name: Elo with jointly estimated item difficulty (computerised adaptive testing)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Runs Elo on a bipartite graph of participants versus PROBLEMS, updating the participant's ability and the problem's difficulty after every answer, so problems are calibrated on the fly with no pre-testing. Item selection targets a success probability near 0.75 (or, in classical CAT, maximum Fisher information at the current ability estimate, which is the item whose difficulty matches current ability). Elo's constant K is replaced by an uncertainty function, e.g. U(n) = a/(1 + b*n) with n the number of previous answers.
mechanisms.citation: Klinkenberg, S., Straatemeier, M. and van der Maas, H.L.J., 'Computer adaptive practice of maths ability using a new item response model for on the fly ability and difficulty estimation', Computers & Education 57(2):1813-1824, 2011. Pelánek, R., 'Applications of the Elo Rating System in Adaptive Educational Systems', Computers & Education, 2016, DOI 10.1016/j.compedu.2016.03.017. Classical maximum-Fisher-information item selection: Lord, F.M., Applications of Item Response Theory to Practical Testing Problems, 1980; van der Linden, W.J., 1998.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: This is the published form of the founder's FIRST mechanism, and it gives him a number. Pelánek's simulation (Rasch model, abilities and difficulties from a standard normal): once item difficulties are well estimated, 'just 10 answers per student are sufficient to produce reasonable skill estimates (correlation 0.8 with' the truth). So 10 calibrated problems per model buys a correlation of 0.8 — the founder's recursive ladder is unnecessary if the problem bank is calibrated. CAT's measured payoff is the same precision 'with as few as half the number of items required of linear tests'.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Handles it by matching problem difficulty to estimated ability, which is exactly the founder's 'models that perform less well get a less complex problem'. The information argument is the same p(1-p) one: an item far from a participant's ability is nearly uninformative. Pelánek also notes 'it may be useful to use different uncertainty function for items and for students' — in CDSFL terms, problems and models should have different learning rates.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers, but with a measured warning that falsifies the naive version of his mechanism. Pelánek's result: 'in the case of adaptive selection of items the proportion correct method gives poor estimates. The quality of these estimates moreover does not improve with the increasing number of students.' So if CDSFL recursively gives easier problems to weaker models and then ranks models by raw solve rate, the ranking is biased AND the bias does not wash out with more data. It must use a joint ability-plus-difficulty model. The good news: Elo with an uncertainty function 'gives nearly the same estimates as joint maximum likelihood, which is a much more computationally demanding procedure', and 'principled approaches to modeling uncertainty actually do not bring significant advantages' over U(n) = a/(1 + b*n) with a = 1, b = 0.05 as a starting point. One more caution: a randomly GENERATED problem has unknown difficulty, so its difficulty parameter starts cold too, and CDSFL would be estimating two cold parameters from one observation.

mechanisms.name: Rating inflation, deflation, floors, and the identifiability limit
mechanisms.what_it_does: The empirical and structural account of what happens to a rating pool over years. Bradley-Terry strengths are identified only up to a multiplicative constant (hence Ford's 1'w = 1 normalisation), so ratings measure DIFFERENCES within a pool and carry no absolute anchor. The documented consequences: inflation when a cohort enters above its strength, deflation when it enters below, and administrative patches — rating floors, raised K-factors, one-time compressions.
mechanisms.citation: Sonas, J., 'Sonas Proposal: Repairing the FIDE Standard Elo rating system', FIDE, 2023, https://www.fide.com/docs/presentations/Sonas%20Proposal%20-%20Repairing%20the%20FIDE%20Standard%20Elo%20Rating%20System.pdf, plus his Supplemental Report. Glickman, M.E. and Doan, T., 'The US Chess Rating system', revised September 2020, https://new.uschess.org/sites/default/files/media/documents/the-us-chess-rating-system-revised-september-2020.pdf (absolute floor 100; established after more than 25 games; floors at 100, 1400, 1500, ..., 2100; 2200 floor for an Original Life Master requiring an established rating above 2200 for 300 rated games). Ford, L.R., 1957, for the normalisation. Critique of the floor: Milvang, O.K., response to Sonas, 2023.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: The USCF answer is a two-regime system: a special algorithm for 8 or fewer games, the standard algorithm thereafter, a provisional label for the first 25 games, and established status from game 26. That is a published, battle-tested answer to 'when may I trust this rating': after roughly 25 games — which agrees to within a factor of 2 with my Glicko computation of 48 games to RD 50.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Floors are the explicit heterogeneity patch and also the explicit lock-in device. A player's floor is roughly their peak established rating minus 200, rounded down to the nearest floor level. It guarantees a rating cannot fall — which is precisely the 'earned its position in the Premier league and cannot be demoted' failure the founder is worried about, implemented ON PURPOSE.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the precise answer to his lock-in question, and it has two halves. HALF ONE, the reassuring half: within-pool lock-in is solved by uncertainty. Glicko's RD grows on inactivity as min(sqrt(RD_old^2 + c^2*t), 350) — Glickman's worked example sets c = 63.2 so that a typical RD-50 player returns to RD 350 in 30 rating periods — and Glicko-2's volatility rises on 'exceptionally strong results after a period of stability'. Glickman names the residual lock-in himself and prescribes the fix: 'when a player competes very frequently, his/her rating stops changing appreciably... This may sometimes prevent a player's rating from changing substantially when the player is truly improving. I would therefore recommend that an RD never drop below a threshold value, such as 30, so that ratings can change appreciably even in a relatively short time.' CDSFL should set an RD floor. HALF TWO, the half he will not like: if the WHOLE population improves 10-fold, no relative rating system detects it, because adding a constant to every strength leaves every win probability unchanged. The measured instance: Sonas found a pool-wide drift where 1500-rated players' scores against 2100-rated players had 'nearly doubled since 2012', requiring a one-time compression of the 1400-2000 band plus a 1400 floor, effective 1 March 2024 [VERIFY:current]. The only cure is an EXTERNAL anchor — a frozen, independently calibrated reference set that does not improve. For CDSFL that means a held-back bank of problems with fixed, separately-validated difficulty, re-run periodically. Nothing in the update rule can substitute for it.

mechanisms.name: Manipulability of score-group pairing (the Swiss Gambit) and provable incentive alignment
mechanisms.what_it_does: Measures whether a participant can improve its final rank by deliberately losing early, since a loss drops it into a weaker score group and therefore easier later opponents. Simulated with the official FIDE pairing system and Milvang's Elo-based outcome distribution.
mechanisms.citation: Cseh, Á., Führlich, P. and Lenzner, P., 'The Swiss Gambit', arXiv:2302.10595, 21 February 2023 (AAMAS 2023). Formal counterpart: Ebtekar and Liu, Theorem 5.5 (Aligned Incentives) and Theorem 5.6 (Memoryless Monotonicity), WWW 2021.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Not its subject, but it establishes the boundary condition for adaptive pairing: the manipulation only pays when outcomes are highly predictable, which is the opposite of the cold-start regime. During cold start, adaptive pairing is safe from this attack.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Measured to matter: 'Gambits are more likely to succeed if the players' strengths span a large range' — which is CDSFL's case, a roster from a desktop to a supercomputer. So the risk is higher for CDSFL than for a chess open.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: The honest summary is that this risk is real but bounded: gambits are 'widely possible', but 'profiting from them requires a high degree of predictability of match results', 'even with a successful gambit, the expected rank improvement is small', and 'the impact of gambits on the ranking quality of all players is low in general'. CDSFL does not need to abandon score-group pairing over it. What it SHOULD do is prefer an estimator with a proof: Elo-MMR's Theorem 5.5 states that a participant's current rating is monotonic in each of its past rankings, so placing lower can never help. For a harness whose seats are optimising agents, a proven-monotonic estimator is worth more than a marginally more accurate one.

mechanisms.name: Intransitivity: multidimensional Elo and Nash averaging
mechanisms.what_it_does: Shows that any scalar rating is a uniform average in logit space and therefore cannot represent a cyclic (rock-paper-scissors) component of the pairwise win matrix. Uses the Hodge decomposition to split transitive from cyclic interactions and adds a rank-2k cyclic term (mElo_2k); separately proposes Nash averaging as an evaluation invariant to redundant tasks and agents.
mechanisms.citation: Balduzzi, D., Tuyls, K., Pérolat, J. and Graepel, T., 'Re-evaluating Evaluation', NeurIPS 2018, pp. 3272-3283; arXiv:1806.02643. Critique of Elo's additivity: Bertrand, Q. et al., 'On the Limitations of Elo: Real-World Games are Transitive, not Additive', arXiv:2206.12301. Clone-manipulability of mElo: 'Evaluating Agents using Social Choice Theory', arXiv:2312.03121.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Worse than scalar systems: mElo_2k has more parameters to estimate from the same data, and Tang, Wang and Jin measured that in the sparse regime (they use t/N < 1000) 'simpler Elo tends to beat Elo2k and Pairwise despite higher misspecification error', because the extra parameters' regret dominates. On a real arena dataset, Elo2k gave no benefit at all despite the data being dense.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Addresses a different axis of heterogeneity — capability that is not totally ordered, e.g. model A better at proofs, model B better at counterexamples. For CDSFL that is a live possibility, since different seats are genuinely good at different falsification moves.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Worth knowing, not worth building yet. The founder's premise that a single ordering exists is an ASSUMPTION, and a likelihood-ratio test rejected the Bradley-Terry model on all 8 real datasets tested, most with p below 1e-10 and an LLM arena dataset at about 1e-3 (Tang et al. 2025). So CDSFL's roster is probably not strictly transitive. But mElo's extra machinery bought nothing measurable on the dense LLM dataset, mElo has a non-convex loss with no gradient-descent guarantee, it can be manipulated by adding copies of agents, and a later paper reports the published formulation 'contains feedback loops that prevent the mElo rating system from correctly inferring an expected pairwise comparison matrix'. Recommendation: measure the cyclic component (compute the Hodge decomposition of CDSFL's own win matrix as a diagnostic) before spending anything on modelling it.

mechanisms.name: Elo's consistency under non-uniform matchmaking
mechanisms.what_it_does: Analyses Elo as online gradient descent on binary cross-entropy and asks whether its ranking is CONSISTENT when the Bradley-Terry model is wrong and when matchmaking is not uniform. Result: under uniform (product) matchmaking the population Bradley-Terry MLE ranks participants identically to their average win rate (Theorems G.1 and 2), and under strong stochastic transitivity this recovers the true ranking as T grows. Under weak stochastic transitivity the average-win-rate ranking need not be correct. Under ARBITRARY matchmaking, Elo can give inconsistent rankings even on strongly-stochastically-transitive instances, as the learning rate goes to 0 and T goes to infinity.
mechanisms.citation: Tang, S., Wang, Y. and Jin, C., 'Is Elo Rating Reliable? A Study Under Model Misspecification', arXiv:2502.10985, 16 February 2025.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Offers the only guarantee in this literature that survives misspecification and non-stationarity: a regret bound, not a consistency result. Per-round average loss is bounded by C*sqrt(N/T) with eta_t = sqrt(N/t), and cumulative loss decomposes as misspecification error plus regret. In the sparse regime, use the simplest model.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Measured non-trivial matchmaking in the real data — 'stronger players face stronger opponents' — and identified it as a reason the data are neither Bradley-Terry nor stationary. That is CDSFL's regime by design.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the sharpest statement of the central danger and should be read as the governing constraint on CDSFL's whole architecture. CDSFL intends (a) non-uniform, capability-dependent routing and (b) a leaderboard derived from the resulting outcomes. This paper proves those two together can yield an INCONSISTENT ranking that does not fix itself with infinite data or an infinitesimal learning rate. The authors' own conclusion is that Elo 'should not be blindly trusted'. The three available repairs, in order of cost: inverse-probability reweighting of the likelihood (the arena's method), an explicit adaptive-selection correction (Urnings), or reserving a fraction of comparisons for genuinely uniform random pairing so that an unbiased estimate always exists alongside the routed one. The third is the cheapest and I would recommend it as a standing holdout: a measured leaderboard computed only from uniformly-sampled matches, published alongside the operational one, with the gap between them as a monitored quantity.

is_the_wheel_already_invented:
Yes, twice over, and both of his mechanisms have published names and measured performance.

MECHANISM 2 (the random knockout) is single-elimination tournament design with random seeding. It is the oldest format in this literature and the one measured WORST at the job he wants. David (1959), Glenn (1960) and Searls (1963) computed exact winning probabilities for 8 players and found single knockout the least effective of the formats studied at identifying the best participant. Sziklai, Biró and Csató (2022) found the Swiss system beats it at equal match count, specifically at recovering a full ranking. Marchand (2002, JRSS-D 51(2):169-178) found that random versus seeded brackets differ less than expected, so the "names from a bag" part is not the problem — the ELIMINATION is. And a theorem forbids making it fair: a balanced knockout with 8 or more players cannot simultaneously favour stronger participants over weaker ones and treat equally strong participants equally (Vu and Shoham 2011; Arlegi and Dimitrov 2020).

MECHANISM 1 (hard random problem, promote the top, recurse with easier problems) is computerised adaptive testing with on-the-fly item calibration, a field roughly 46 years old in its IRT form and 15 years old in its Elo form. Classical CAT selects the item maximising Fisher information at the current ability estimate, which is the item whose difficulty matches current ability — his recursion, derived from an optimality criterion rather than intuition. Klinkenberg, Straatemeier and van der Maas (2011) built exactly his version: Elo updating ability and item difficulty simultaneously, no pre-testing, items sampled at a mean success probability of 0.75, deployed at a scale of 3648 children completing over 3.5 million arithmetic problems in 10 months.

His COLD-START problem specifically is Glicko's founding motivation. Glickman created Glicko in 1995 for precisely the case where you cannot tell an unknown 1700 from a measured 1700, and the rating deviation is the answer. His LOCK-IN problem specifically is Glicko-2's volatility parameter and TrueSkill's dynamics factor tau, which the reference documentation describes in his own words as "the factor that restrains a fixation of rating".

What is NOT already invented: nothing in this literature rates capability and COST jointly, nothing computes ratings without a central authority, and no system except Urnings corrects for the adaptive selection CDSFL depends on.
strongest_disagreement:
The knockout bracket is not merely suboptimal, it is mathematically unable to produce the ranking he wants, and I can state that as a theorem plus a measurement rather than an opinion.

THE THEOREM. Ford (1957) proved that the Bradley-Terry maximum-likelihood estimate exists and is unique if and only if the directed win graph is strongly connected: for every split of the participants into two non-empty groups, someone in one group must have beaten someone in the other. A single-elimination bracket on n participants produces exactly n-1 matches and an ACYCLIC win graph — every match has a definite winner and no participant ever beats someone who beat them. Strong connectivity therefore cannot hold for n >= 2. His bracket does not produce a hard-to-estimate ranking; it produces one for which the standard estimator is undefined.

THE MEASUREMENT (scripts committed to /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-georgejackson-Developer-Projects/a07b3790-0a2a-4978-aedb-bd842c0493d3/scratchpad/bt_connect_rate.py and bt_knockout.py, 500 simulated 16-player tournaments per configuration, logistic true-skill model, seed 7). Knockout with a random draw: the MLE was defined in 0 of 500 runs, at every upset level tested (logistic scale 2.0, 4.0 and 8.0). Hunter's MM iteration on one such bracket diverged to a max/min strength ratio of 1.6e+301 and kept diverging from 10 to 10000 iterations. A 7-round Swiss on the same 16 participants: 65 of 500 at scale 4.0, 132 of 500 at scale 8.0, 5 of 500 at scale 2.0. A 10-round Swiss: 239 of 500. So Swiss is far better but still unreliable, and the correct conclusion is not "use Swiss" but "never use an unregularised Bradley-Terry MLE" — use a prior, which is what Glicko, TrueSkill, Elo-MMR and the arena's reweighted fit all do and what his design currently lacks.

THE INFORMATION BUDGET. Negahban, Oh and Shah (Operations Research 65(1):266-287, 2017) proved Omega(n log n) random comparisons are necessary for ANY algorithm to produce a consistent ranking, because below that the comparison graph is disconnected with positive probability. A knockout gives n-1. For 700 models that is 699 comparisons against a floor of roughly 4600 — short by a factor of about 6.6, and the shortfall is information-theoretic, not an implementation detail.

THE SECOND DISAGREEMENT, which is more dangerous because it survives switching to Swiss. His whole design routes work by measured capability, which makes the match-up distribution non-uniform and capability-dependent. Tang, Wang and Jin (arXiv:2502.10985, Theorem 2 and the surrounding analysis) prove that under ARBITRARY matchmaking Elo can give inconsistent rankings even on strongly-stochastically-transitive instances, as the learning rate goes to 0 and the number of rounds goes to infinity. Bolsinova, Maris, Hofman, van der Maas and Brinkhuis (JRSS-C 71(1):91-118, 2022) measured the same defect from the other side: adaptive selection inflates rating variance so that "the ratings are diverging from each other over time without converging to a limiting distribution", and they state that Glicko (2001), TrueSkill (2006) and TrueSkill 2 (2018) contain no correction for it. A tiered ladder fed by its own routing decisions is therefore liable to show an ever-widening top tier for reasons that are an artefact of the routing. That is a self-confirming leaderboard — which is the precise thing his "capability is measured, never a name" constraint exists to prevent, arriving through a mechanism his constraint does not block.

THE THIRD, on leagues. Discrete leagues are pure overhead AS AN ESTIMATOR — every production system keeps a continuous rating underneath and shows tiers only as a display layer (Ubisoft's ranked tiers sit on TrueSkill scores; Riot's visible rank sits on an unpublished continuous MMR; FIDE titles sit on a continuous Elo). Discretisation loses information (Medo and Wakeling, arXiv:1001.3745, measured that moving from continuous to discrete rating scales has "a significant impact on algorithms' performance"). Leagues DO have one legitimate function: restricting the pairing pool to near-equals, which is what Glickman and Jensen (2005) proved is information-optimal. But the Swiss SCORE GROUP is the strictly better version of that idea, because it is recomputed every round and therefore cannot lock in, whereas a persistent league plus any floor is lock-in by construction — USCF floors at 100, 1400, 1500 through 2100 exist precisely to stop a rating falling, and Milvang's objection to the 2024 FIDE 1400 floor was that it "divides the players into rated and unrated players". He should build score groups, not leagues.

WHERE HE IS RIGHT, and it should be said. Assuming no capability at the outset is correct, and Glicko implements it exactly (rating 1500, RD 350, a 95% interval of plus or minus 686 points — the system saying in its own units that it knows nothing). Random pairing in round 1 is also correct: under a genuinely exchangeable prior all pairings have identical expected information by symmetry, and FIDE's own Dutch system falls back to lot for round-1 colours. His error is not the start. It is round 2 onward, where the bracket throws away half the roster and random pairing stops being optimal.
open_problems: Cost is absent from every system in this literature. Elo, Glicko, Glicko-2, TrueSkill, TrueSkill 2, Elo-MMR, Bradley-Terry, Plackett-Luce, mElo and Urnings all estimate a scalar (or 2k-dimensional) SKILL. None models the price, latency, memory or energy of obtaining a result, and none treats matches as having unequal cost. The founder's actual objective — capability per unit of resource — has no published rating system behind it. Tournament design assumes every match costs the same; CDSFL's matches differ in cost by orders of magnitude. This is the genuinely novel part of his question and this dimension cannot answer it.

No published rating system computes updates without a central authority. Glicko and Glicko-2 specify a rating period over which one administrator updates all participants in parallel; Swiss pairing requires a pairing authority each round; Elo-MMR is embarrassingly parallel but still single-coordinator. I found nothing in this literature addressing a trustless, peer-to-peer setting where participants report their own results. The nearest adjacent concern is manipulation (the Swiss Gambit; Elo-MMR's incentive-alignment theorem), which assumes honest reporting of outcomes and only asks whether a participant benefits from losing. Self-reported outcomes in a decentralised rating pool is an open problem here.

Efficacy as a function of roster size is explicitly unstudied. Devriesere, Csató and Goossens (arXiv:2404.05034) state that 'the effect of the number of participants (n) on efficacy is still a blind spot'. The efficacy studies cited run at 8, 16 or 32 participants. The founder requires 1, 5, 6, 70 and 700 without redesign, and there is no published measurement of how format efficacy behaves at 700. TrueSkill is separately measured to degrade above about 60 distinct ranks in one round, which is a warning rather than an answer.

Adaptive selection correction exists in exactly one algorithm, for the wrong data type. Urnings corrects for adaptive item selection, but it is formulated for binary-response person-versus-item comparisons in educational measurement. Extending it to multi-participant ranked rounds (CDSFL's actual observation unit), to partial rankings, and to cost-weighted outcomes is unpublished work. Glicko, TrueSkill and TrueSkill 2 have no such correction, and their authors do not claim one.

There is no principled answer to the uniform-population-improvement problem within the rating machinery. Because Bradley-Terry strengths are identified only up to a constant, a pool in which everyone improves equally shows no rating movement at all. Every remedy in the record is administrative and external: FIDE's one-time compression of the 1400-2000 band, the 1400 floor, raised K-factors, a frozen anchor set. Nobody has published a rating system that detects pool-wide drift from internal evidence alone. For CDSFL this means a calibrated, frozen reference bank is a REQUIREMENT, not an optimisation, and the design of such a bank (how many items, how often refreshed, how to prevent contamination of the bank by the models being measured) is open.

The tension between the two optimal-pairing criteria is unresolved. Glickman and Jensen (2005) say pair participants whose capability is close and whose uncertainty is large. Negahban, Oh and Shah (2017) say the sample complexity degrades as the inverse square of the comparison graph's spectral gap, which near-equal pairing damages by fragmenting the graph into weakly-linked clusters. No paper I found jointly optimises information gain and graph connectivity. The practical consequence for CDSFL is that it must hold back some fraction of comparisons for deliberately cross-tier pairings, and the right fraction is unknown.

A falsification-harness outcome is not an exogenous win. Every system here takes the match result as given data. In CDSFL the 'win' is itself a contestable artefact — a proof that may be wrong, a falsifier that may not execute, a fix that may not cure. Rating systems with verified-but-contestable outcomes, where the outcome itself can later be overturned and the ratings must be recomputed, are not addressed. The nearest thing is the arena's immutable vote log plus batch re-estimation, which at least makes retrospective correction possible — an argument for a batch estimator over an online one.

Whether the roster is transitive at all is unmeasured for CDSFL. A likelihood-ratio test rejected Bradley-Terry on all 8 real datasets Tang, Wang and Jin examined, most at p below 1e-10. If CDSFL's seats are genuinely non-transitive on falsification tasks, a single ordering is the wrong object and the tiered-league premise fails at the root. The cheap diagnostic (compute the Hodge decomposition of CDSFL's own observed win matrix and measure the cyclic component's magnitude) has not been run and should be, before any ladder is built on the assumption that one exists.
